Analytic tests and real carriers

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0.

A distribution at a point reads finitely many derivatives. An analytic functional at a point can read infinitely many, provided its coefficients decrease fast enough. To make this a local theory on real sets, we must first show that a functional initially defined on entire functions can act on a function holomorphic only near its carrier. The central construction below gives that extension by an explicit Gaussian approximation. In one complex variable, regular simple arcs give minimal complex carriers; polynomial approximation distinguishes a genuine carrier from a path image containing a loop.

We use bilinear pairings and ordinary derivatives. The supplied Cauchy reading, CX7–CX11 and CMI6–CMI8, proves the Cauchy formula, derivative bounds and convergent several-variable Taylor expansions. Functional foundations, BF1–BF2, supplies the metric for a countable family of seminorms. Integration foundations, Sections 15–16, supplies dominated convergence, Fubini and substitution. Cutoffs, compactness and elementary derivative rules are in metric foundations, Sections 12–13. The normalized Gaussian and its Fourier transform are proved in Fourier foundations, F3.

The exact smooth contour identity used below is supplied as an AN-04 programme proof. The distribution comparisons use compact pairings, Theorem 3.1, and point-supported distributions, Theorems 1.1 and 3.1. These are available proofs, with their original authorship retained.

Entire tests and a complete space

Let be a nonempty compact subset of , . An analytic functional carried by is a complex-linear map on entire functions such that for every open neighborhood of , It suffices to use bounded neighborhoods; restriction to a smaller one gives the estimate for a larger one. Write this space as , and set . A carrier is a set for which (A1) holds; it is not initially a uniquely determined support.

Put and These finite seminorms increase with , and they separate functionals. In fact each is a norm, since every entire function is bounded on the closure of . The neighborhoods are cofinal among neighborhoods of : a finite ball cover of the compact set supplies a positive distance to the complement of any prescribed neighborhood.

Theorem 1 (completeness and polynomial determination). The seminorms (A2) make a complete metrizable locally convex space. A functional is determined by its values on polynomials. Conversely, a linear functional on polynomials satisfying (A1) for every neighborhood extends uniquely to .

Proof. The metric has the stated topology, and a sequence is Cauchy for it exactly when it is Cauchy for every , by BF1–BF2. Suppose is such a sequence. For each entire , the estimate using shows that is Cauchy. Its limit is linear. For fixed , the numbers are bounded, so passage to the limit in (A1) gives a finite . If for , take to infinity for each test and then the supremum to get . Thus .

The Taylor polynomials of an entire function converge uniformly on each bounded set: enclose it in a smaller concentric polydisk than one on which the Cauchy coefficients are estimated, and sum the resulting geometric series, as in CMI8. Therefore (A1) determines from polynomial values. For the converse, apply the polynomial estimate on any fixed bounded neighborhood to the differences of Taylor polynomials. Their functional values are Cauchy. The limit is linear, has the same estimate on that neighborhood, and is independent of polynomial approximations converging uniformly on every compact set. Repeating for every neighborhood proves (A1) and uniqueness.

Theorem 2 (all measurements at one point). With multi-indices , a functional belongs to exactly when The coefficients are uniquely , and the series is absolutely convergent on every holomorphic germ at zero.

Proof. Apply (A1) to the monomial on a polydisk of radius to obtain the bound. Theorem 1 then gives the series on entire functions. Conversely, if is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed polydisk of radius , its coefficients satisfy Choose . The sum of is , so (A4) converges absolutely and is bounded by . Every neighborhood of zero contains such a polydisk. This proves (A1), including the asserted germ action. Testing monomials proves uniqueness.

Local holomorphic tests

A holomorphic germ near is represented by a function holomorphic on some neighborhood of ; two representatives agree if they agree on a possibly smaller neighborhood.

Theorem 5 (extension and holomorphic parameters). Every , for real compact , has a unique linear extension to holomorphic germs near such that for every neighborhood of , If is jointly holomorphic near , then is holomorphic near , and its derivatives are obtained by differentiating .

Proof. Choose with . Theorem 4 gives entire uniformly there. A bound (A1) on a smaller open neighborhood inside makes Cauchy. Define as its limit. For two choices, use a smaller contained in both neighborhoods and in the region where the representatives agree. The difference of their approximants tends uniformly to zero there, proving independence. This also proves linearity. Applying the bound on a fixed smaller neighborhood and passing to the limit yields (L1), with a constant depending only on the chosen neighborhood, not on .

Any extension with (L1) has the same limit on these approximants, so it is unique. More precisely, take a smaller open neighborhood whose closure is contained in ; convergence there makes (L1) applicable to the difference.

For the parameter assertion, compactness of gives a parameter polydisk and a fixed complex neighborhood of on whose product is holomorphic. The parameter Taylor series, and each derivative series on a smaller polydisk, converge uniformly in on a smaller closed neighborhood of , by CMI8. Apply the bound for term by term. The resulting convergent power series proves both assertions.

The same parameter conclusion holds for a complex compact carrier when the functions in the carrier variable are entire and the parameter series converges uniformly on every fixed bounded neighborhood used in (A1). No assertion about local germs at arbitrary complex compact sets is needed.

Which analytic functionals are distributions?

Theorem 6 (faithful distribution inclusion and real carriers). A compactly supported distribution defines an analytic functional . For a real compact set , The map is injective. In particular, (A4) represents a compactly supported distribution exactly when only finitely many are nonzero.

Proof. Suppose . On a fixed real compact neighborhood of , the compact pairing theorem bounds by finitely many derivatives after a cutoff. Given a complex neighborhood of , choose the real cutoff with support sufficiently close to , and a uniform polydisk radius about its support contained in . The Cauchy derivative estimates and the finite Leibniz rule bound by . This proves the forward implication. The extension in Theorem 5 agrees with the ordinary compact distribution pairing on holomorphic germs: uniform holomorphic approximation on a larger neighborhood gives convergence of all finitely many needed derivatives on a smaller one, by the Cauchy estimates.

For the reverse implication, take , and put These functions are entire. On the real domain, integration by parts moves each derivative to . The normalized real Gaussians form an approximate identity: split the integral into , where uniform continuity bounds the translated difference, and , whose Gaussian mass tends to zero. Apply this to each derivative of . Hence in every finite derivative norm, and .

Let , and choose . If , then for , Consequently , where is this fixed neighborhood of . Applying (A1) gives . This proves the reverse implication in (D1). If , the same real approximate-identity argument for arbitrary compact smooth gives , proving injectivity.

If (A4) comes from a compact distribution, (D1) puts its support at zero. The point specialization of the earlier jet theorem says it is a finite linear combination of derivatives of , so its monomial values eventually vanish. Conversely, finitely many coefficients give the distribution Its pairing is precisely (A4).

For example, in one variable, is an analytic functional carried by zero and is not a distribution. Indeed satisfies (A4), since by the exponential series, and infinitely many coefficients are nonzero.

Operations on carriers

Proposition 7 (local operations and transport). The following constructions are well defined.

  1. For any compact complex carrier , differentiation is and preserves .
  2. For real compact and an analytic germ near , multiplication is and preserves the carrier.
  3. If , , with complex compact carriers, there is a tensor . Both orders of iterated pairing agree. For real carriers the same holds for holomorphic germs near .
  4. For real compact and a real analytic map near , belongs to . If is a real analytic diffeomorphism, , and , its distribution-convention pullback is
  5. For real carriers, convolution is the pushforward of under , and is carried by . If , compact, and is analytic near the second projection of , then is carried by the first projection of .

These operations agree with the corresponding operations on compact distributions.

Proof. For differentiation, given , choose a smaller bounded neighborhood and a fixed polydisk radius with the polydisks about its points contained in . The Cauchy estimate bounds by . Apply the bound for on . For local germs the same formula follows by Theorem 5 and derivative convergence on smaller neighborhoods. Multiplication follows from that theorem and the bound for on a smaller closed neighborhood of . The product rule therefore also gives .

Define the tensor first on a polynomial . Finite sums show that the two orders of pairing agree. On bounded neighborhoods , , successive application of (A1) gives Every neighborhood of contains such a product of sufficiently small neighborhoods: a positive distance from the compact product to its complement supplies them. Theorem 1 extends the tensor to entire functions. Uniform polynomial approximation on the chosen product, together with the parameter conclusion of Theorem 5 in its entire-variable form, identifies both iterated pairings. For real carriers, Theorem 4 applied in variables approximates a local germ uniformly on a complex neighborhood of ; on a smaller product neighborhood the same bounds identify both iterated extensions. This also proves associativity of tensors by first checking polynomials.

A real analytic map has a holomorphic extension as a germ near each real compact subset of its domain. Its local power series give the extensions; on overlaps they agree near the real set because their difference has all real Taylor coefficients zero there. Shrinking and using a finite cover gives a common germ. Given a neighborhood of , continuity puts the image of a sufficiently small neighborhood of inside it. Theorem 5 then proves the bound for .

For (O1), the nonvanishing real determinant has locally constant sign, so its absolute value is a real analytic germ. Apply multiplication followed by the pushforward under . This proves the asserted carrier and normalization. The sum map gives convolution. In (O2), choose a small neighborhood of on which is bounded and the first projection lies in a prescribed neighborhood of its compact image; Theorem 5 supplies the required bound.

For distributions, the germ pairing agrees with their compact pairing by Theorem 6. Each displayed definition is then the usual one. Tensor agreement follows first on entire tests, using polynomial approximation and finite derivative bounds, and then injectivity in Theorem 6; compact distribution tensors and convolution were proved in the earlier tensor and convolution lessons. The ordinary change-of-variables formula supplies exactly the absolute Jacobian in (O1).

Entire transforms remember the functional

For real compact , let .

Theorem 8 (Fourier–Laplace transform). For , the function is entire, determines , and for every satisfies Here the norms are Euclidean, also for complex vectors.

Proof. The parameter statement of Theorem 5 gives holomorphy and For , choose with . The real part of is at most , by the complex Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (the real coordinate square inequality proves it). Apply (A1) on this neighborhood to obtain (F2). If two transforms agree, (F3) gives identical monomial values, so Theorem 1 gives identical functionals.

The theorem proves a necessary growth estimate and uniqueness. A characterization of which entire functions satisfying (F2) arise as transforms requires a further existence argument. Likewise, completeness for a fixed carrier in Theorem 1 does not yet assert completeness modulo functionals carried by a smaller set.

Paths, polynomial approximation and minimal complex carriers

We now work in one complex variable. A carrier of a nonzero functional is minimal if none of its proper compact subsets is a carrier. This differs from a smallest carrier, which must be contained in every carrier. Complex carriers can have several incomparable minimal members.

We need polynomial approximation on planar compact sets, including disconnected ones. The proof uses the contour integral and triangle theorem CX1–CX4, the Cauchy estimates CX6–CX9, and the rectangle index calculation in Section 6 of the Cauchy reading.

Lemma 9 (polynomial approximation on a neighborhood). Let be compact, with connected complement, and let be an open neighborhood of . There is a compact such that If is holomorphic on , polynomials can be chosen with On every compact subset of , every fixed derivative converges uniformly as well. The empty set causes no restriction.

Proof: compact neighborhoods without holes. Assume , and choose with . An open connected subset of the plane is polygonally connected: the points reachable from a fixed point by a finite polygonal path in the open set form a nonempty relatively open set, and their complement is relatively open too, since a small ball can be joined by straight segments. Connectedness makes the reachable set the whole open set.

Put . This is a compact subset of . From each , choose a polygonal path in that complement to a point outside , and continue radially to infinity. The radial continuation avoids . The compact initial path has positive distance from ; a sufficiently small ball about joins to that same path by straight segments with a positive distance from . A finite collection of these balls covers . Consequently, for some , every point of lies in the unbounded component of , where Decrease so that . If is empty, only this last condition is needed. The exterior of is connected, so the complement of has exactly one unbounded component . Components of an open set are open, by the same small-ball argument. Thus is closed and bounded. It contains , and misses and the exterior of the large disk. Therefore , proving (P1).

Proof: Cauchy sums with finitely many poles. For any compact , choose a square grid of sufficiently small mesh and take the finite union of all its closed cells meeting a small closed neighborhood of . The mesh and neighborhood can be chosen so that and . The exterior edges, with their inherited orientations, form a finite chain at positive distance from . Each shared edge cancels with its oppositely oriented copy.

For off the grid lines, apply the Cauchy formula in each cell and add. The cell containing contributes ; the others contribute zero. To obtain that rectangular formula directly, subtract , divide by , use the point-removal triangle argument CX3–CX5, and apply the inside/outside rectangle index calculation. Continuity on includes its grid-line points, and therefore every point of , even if has no off-grid points nearby. Hence The kernel is jointly continuous on the finite edge chain times . Its Riemann sums converge uniformly on , because uniform continuity bounds every summand's error by its edge length times a common modulus of continuity. These sums are rational functions with finitely many poles in .

Proof: moving every pole to polynomial approximation. Let be the uniform closure on of polynomials. It is a closed algebra: uniform convergence preserves sums, and the uniformly bounded factors make products converge uniformly. Let It contains every sufficiently large , by the uniformly convergent expansion . If and , then converges uniformly on ; every finite sum belongs to . Thus is relatively open. If tends to , their kernels converge uniformly on , so . Thus is relatively closed. The connectedness in (P1) gives . Every rational Cauchy sum in (P4) therefore belongs to , and so does . This proves (P2).

Finally, if , choose so that every closed disk of radius centered in lies in . CX9 gives The same sequence works for every fixed .

Theorem 11 (a path functional and all simple-arc minimal carriers). Let be complex numbers. For an entire , define along the straight segment. Every path from to gives the same value and has its compact image as a carrier. If the path is injective with nonvanishing derivative, its image is a minimal carrier.

Proof: independence and a carrier estimate. The Taylor series has the entire primitive , by uniform convergence and differentiation on compact disks. The real chain rule and fundamental theorem give the integral along any path as . If its image is , then for every neighborhood , This is exactly the carrier condition. Also .

Proof: no proper compact subset of a simple arc carries it. Let be a proper compact subset of an injective regular arc . Since is closed and proper, its complement contains an interior parameter . This remains true if an initially missing point was an endpoint, by continuity and closedness. Choose The two compact subarcs are disjoint, , , and . Corollary 12 (two minimal carriers and a nonminimal path image). The upper and lower semicircles are incomparable minimal carriers of . Their intersection is not a carrier, so this functional has no smallest complex carrier. Regularity of a parametrized path alone does not imply minimality of its image.

Proof. Both parametrizations in (P17) are injective and have derivative of constant modulus . Their imaginary parts have opposite strict signs in the interior, so their intersection is exactly the two endpoints. Theorem 11 proves minimality; either arc's proper subset therefore cannot be a carrier. A smallest carrier would be contained in this intersection, and enlarging a carrier preserves the carrier estimate, a contradiction.

For the last assertion, use the path on Both values at the join are zero and both derivatives are ; on the circle , while on the segment it is . Thus is with nonvanishing derivative. It traverses the circle of center and radius , then the segment . The circle contributes zero by the entire primitive, and the segment alone is already a carrier. Its image is therefore not minimal. An affine increasing reparametrization places the example on without changing these conclusions.

Exercise 1 — an infinite point measurement. Evaluate (D5) on , and show directly that its value is entire in .

Solution. The value is . On , its absolute sum is at most , and each derivative series is uniformly convergent on smaller disks by the same factorial estimate. Thus it is entire. Its infinitely many nonzero moments show, by Theorem 6, that it is not a distribution.

Exercise 3 — why complex carriers need care. In one complex variable show that evaluation at zero has both and the unit circle as carriers. Explain the failure of intersection here.

Solution. The point carrier is immediate. The Cauchy formula on the unit circle gives , so , which is bounded by the supremum on every neighborhood of the circle. The two compact carriers are disjoint, while evaluation at zero is nonzero. It is therefore not carried by their empty intersection. Both sets are complex carriers; the real-carrier approximation theorem does not assert this example has a second disjoint real carrier.
